name: Nasal fat grafting

card.summary: Injecting a person's own processed fat into the nose to smooth the dorsum, soften contours and add volume, often as a rhinoplasty adjunct.
card.note: Surgical procedure; graft survival varies and complications are possible.

quick.overview:
Nasal fat grafting moves a patient's own fat, usually harvested by liposuction, into the nose. It is used to fill soft defects of the dorsum, lift a low nasal tip or soften a tight nasal envelope, so the nose looks smoother and better contoured.

A randomized controlled trial comparing fat grafting with hyaluronic acid filler found 73.7% of fat-graft patients had excellent cosmetic results at one year, versus 29.7% for filler; the trial was small and drew published criticism of its methods.
quick.how: The procedure has three stages: harvesting fat, processing it and re-injecting it into the nose, performed under local or general anaesthesia. It is used by itself or alongside rhinoplasty, including as pre-treatment before revision surgery on contracted noses.
quick.risks: Reported complications of fat grafting in general include swelling, bruising, donor-site pain, infection, contour irregularities and fat necrosis, and part of the graft may be reabsorbed.

lead: Nasal fat grafting, sometimes called rhinofiller with fat, uses a patient's own fat to improve the nose's contour. Wikipedia notes that micro fat transplantation is used to correct a low nasal dorsum and short nose.[1]

A 2023 randomized trial in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery compared fat grafting with hyaluronic acid for soft defects of the dorsum, low boxy tip and hidden columella; at one year, 73.7% of fat-graft patients showed excellent cosmetic results compared with 29.7% in the filler group, though patients found HA injection more comfortable.[2] A published comment raised reservations about the study's methods.[3]
In revision rhinoplasty for severely contracted noses in Asian patients, autologous lipo-aspirated fat combined with mechanical stretch has been used before surgery to soften the nasal envelope.[4]

angle.text: It fills small soft-tissue irregularities and softens contours, with results that can be visible at one year.

paras: Fat transfer has three stages: harvesting, processing and reinjection, and the graft should be handled minimally and reinjected quickly. Up to half of transferred fat may be reabsorbed in some uses.[1]
Fat grafting in general can cause swelling, bruising, hematoma, numbness, donor-site pain, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities and fat necrosis.[1]

The 2023 randomized trial compared 15 fat-graft patients with 17 hyaluronic acid patients and followed them to a year and beyond; fat grafting patients had higher satisfaction with nasal contour at one year, while HA was rated more comfortable.[2] A letter criticised aspects of the methodology.[3] A study of 24 patients with contracted noses combined fat and stretch before revision rhinoplasty, with a six-month follow-up.[4]
